strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: using interaction already collected during deployment to improve subsequent medical image segmentation under distribution shift.

The two-stage adaptation procedure is simple and well motivated, separating segmentation with a localization click from refinement with correction clicks. It requires only two parameter updates per image.

Experiments cover multiple fundus datasets and MRI modality/pathology shifts, with substantial improvements in several challenging settings. For example, one-click BRATS T1 Dice improves from 35.1 with TSCA to 59.6, and ten-click ATLAS Dice improves from 64.0 to 81.8.

Using the same pretrained backbone for the main adaptation baselines helps isolate adaptation effects. The compute-matched Stage1 ×2 ablation, held-out adaptation trajectory, and three-click experiments provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited relative to existing continuous interactive adaptation. The contribution combines hard pseudo-label self-training, two prompt configurations, and spatially weighted cross-entropy. The paper does not sufficiently establish why this combination constitutes a substantial advance beyond the application and reported gains.

The evaluation substantially simplifies clinical interaction. All clicks are simulated using ground-truth error regions, and MRI evaluation uses only the slice with the largest ground-truth lesion area per case. This excludes much of the difficulty of volumetric segmentation, small lesions, and realistic user behavior. No clinician study or click-noise robustness experiment supports the clinical-workflow claims.

Evidence for reliable continuous adaptation is incomplete. Stream ordering, sensitivity to permutations, and model reset conventions across datasets are not clearly documented. Table 1 reports three-run averages without variability, while repetition details for the MRI experiments are unclear. Aggregate Dice does not establish stability or characterize failure cases under severe shifts.

Component validation is confined to G1020 cup segmentation. There are no corresponding ablations on the MRI settings responsible for the largest gains, no matched comparison against sparse click loss or uniformly weighted local supervision, and no sensitivity analysis for the Gaussian radius, sigma, or loss weight. The contribution of GPL during pretraining versus online adaptation is also not isolated.

The method treats its own final prediction as a hard target, and synthetic correction clicks are derived from that same target. This can reinforce segmentation errors rather than correct them. The claim that general segmentation ability is preserved because unchanged regions remain in the pseudo-label is not guaranteed by parameter updates; pseudo-label error propagation needs direct analysis.

Baseline coverage and practical-efficiency evidence are incomplete. IA+SA is omitted from all MRI experiments based on fundus results, and the Medical SAM Adapter training and prompting protocol is insufficiently described. Counting backpropagations does not establish interactive latency without accounting for forward passes, click generation, and measured runtime.

Reproducibility is limited by missing preprocessing and image-resolution details, base-model training schedules, click encoding and multiclass implementation details, and hyperparameter-selection procedures. These omissions are particularly consequential for a loss defined using fixed pixel distances. Code and models are promised only upon publication.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant problem: using corrections from interactive segmentation to improve performance on subsequent images under distribution shift.

Reports substantial improvements over relevant adaptation baselines across multiple datasets. For example, one-click Dice on BRATS T1 increases from 35.1 with TSCA to 59.6, and ten-click Dice on ATLAS increases from 64.0 to 81.8.

The two-stage procedure is straightforward and reportedly requires only two backpropagation steps per image. Using the same pretrained backbone for the main adaptation comparisons helps isolate the adaptation strategy.
The ablations include a useful computation-matched Stage1 ×2 control and a held-out evaluation of adaptation progress, providing some evidence for the complementary roles of the two stages.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited relative to the acknowledged prior work on continuous interactive adaptation. The main additions are distillation from many-click predictions into a one-click model, synthetic corrective clicks, and spatially weighted pseudo-label cross-entropy. The paper does not sufficiently establish why this combination constitutes a substantial methodological advance.

The central supervision assumption is insufficiently examined. Final predictions after a fixed click budget are treated as dense ground truth, although considerable errors remain under severe shifts. Stage 2 then generates clicks from those same pseudo-labels. There is no direct analysis of error reinforcement or adaptation failures. Moreover, GPL excludes pixels whose pseudo-label disagrees with the click class, so it does not necessarily enforce actual user corrections when the pseudo-label is wrong.

The ablations are confined to G1020 cup segmentation, leaving the mechanisms behind the larger MRI gains unverified. Removing GPL does not establish that Gaussian weighting itself matters: comparisons with sparse click loss, uniform neighborhood weighting, or alternative pseudo-label weighting are missing. Sensitivity to the Gaussian width, neighborhood size, and loss weight is also unreported.

The evaluation does not substantiate the clinical reliability claims. All interactions are simulated using ground-truth error regions, and MRI evaluation selects only the largest-lesion slice per case using annotations. This is a useful controlled benchmark, but excludes full-volume segmentation, lesion-free slices, and realistic user variability. No clinician study or robustness evaluation with inaccurate clicks is provided.

Evidence for stable continuous adaptation is incomplete. Results largely summarize averages over target-domain sequences, without systematic assessment of ordering sensitivity, changing target distributions, or worst-case degradation. Table 1 averages some methods over three runs but provides no uncertainty; comparable replication details are not supplied for the MRI experiments. Small improvements therefore remain difficult to assess.

Reproducibility and comparison details are insufficient. Image preprocessing and resolution, source-training schedules, click encoding, sequence ordering, and baseline hyperparameter-selection procedures are underspecified. The Medical SAM Adapter comparison lacks enough training and prompting detail to interpret its poor results. Code is only promised after publication, and the efficiency claim relies on backward-pass counts without measured latency or memory. Together with the limited novelty and validation gaps, these issues place the paper below the acceptance threshold despite promising empirical gains.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: learning continuously from corrections made during interactive medical image segmentation. Separately improving initial segmentation and responsiveness to subsequent clicks is well motivated.

Experiments cover multiple fundus datasets, MRI modalities, and brain pathologies. Several improvements over TSCA are substantial: one-click Dice increases from 35.1 to 59.6 on BRATS T1, and ten-click Dice increases from 64.0 to 81.8 on ATLAS.

Using the same pretrained interactive backbone for the main adaptation comparisons helps isolate the adaptation strategy. The frozen baseline and experiments with three clicks provide additional useful evidence.

The ablations include individual stages, a computation-matched Stage1 ×2 variant, and removal of GPL. Evaluation on a held-out portion of G1020 provides evidence that adaptation benefits subsequent images.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is incremental relative to existing continuous interactive adaptation. The main additions are distillation from a corrected prediction into a single-click prediction and spatially weighted pseudo-label cross-entropy. The paper does not sufficiently establish why Gaussian weighting is essential compared with sparse click supervision or uniformly weighted local neighborhoods.

Evidence isolating the proposed components is limited to G1020 cup segmentation. The much larger MRI gains are not accompanied by corresponding ablations, and sensitivity to Gaussian width, loss weight, pseudo-label quality, and stream ordering is unexplored. These omissions weaken the generality of the claimed mechanism.

Clinical applicability is only indirectly evaluated. All interactions are simulated using ground-truth error regions, and MRI experiments select the single slice with the largest lesion area using annotations. This excludes much of the difficulty of volumetric segmentation, small lesions, and realistic clinician interaction. Click perturbation or user studies would strengthen the practical claims.

Reliability under continuous adaptation is insufficiently characterized. Table 1 reports three-run averages without variability, while repetition details for the remaining experiments are unclear. There are no confidence intervals, substantive failure analyses, or evaluations of changing distributions within a stream. Self-training on imperfect corrected masks can reinforce errors, and the claim that unchanged pseudo-label regions preserve general segmentation ability is not guaranteed by shared parameter updates.

Reproducibility and comparison details are incomplete: image resolution and preprocessing, base-model training schedules, click encoding, multiclass click handling, stream construction, and hyperparameter-selection protocols are not adequately specified. The Medical SAM adapter comparison also lacks sufficient training and prompting details. Code and models are promised only upon publication.

The efficiency argument counts backpropagations but provides no wall-clock latency, memory measurements, or hardware specification. This supports a narrower computational claim than the paper's assertions about practical deployment.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: using interactive corrections to improve medical segmentation across deployment-time distribution shifts. Combining learning within an interaction with learning across images is well motivated.

Reported improvements are substantial across multiple datasets and shift types. At 10 clicks, OAIMS improves Dice over TSCA from 74.0 to 88.0 on BraTS T1 and from 64.0 to 86.0 on ATLAS. Comparisons against adaptation baselines use the same pretrained backbone, including CCG pretraining.

The evaluation includes extensive component ablations, reduced click budgets, noisy clicks, mixed distributions, source-domain revisiting, and comparisons with ordinary pseudo-labeling and entropy minimization. These provide meaningful evidence beyond aggregate benchmark gains.

The method is computationally simple, with reported low adaptation latency. The clicks-to-target experiment also supports potential interaction savings, reducing the average clicks to 80% Dice on BraTS T1 from 10.60 to 4.43.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The manuscript omits training and adaptation learning rates, optimizer configuration, training duration, detailed U-Net architecture, image resolution and preprocessing, and most dataset sample counts. Baseline tuning procedures are insufficiently documented, and code is only promised after publication. These omissions are particularly consequential for online methods whose stability depends on optimization settings.

Clinical generalization is evaluated narrowly. MRI experiments select only the ground-truth-largest lesion slice per patient, excluding much of the difficulty of full-volume segmentation, small lesions, and lesion-free slices. All interactions are simulated using ground truth; there is no clinician study validating the assumption that fixed-budget outputs are satisfactory pseudo-labels. The results support the simulated setting more strongly than the clinical deployment claims.

Main results lack uncertainty estimates across training seeds, click realizations, and image orders. Some supplementary experiments mention three runs, but do not report dispersion. Aggregate sequence averages also obscure adaptation speed and early failures. These omissions limit assessment of smaller improvements and robustness claims.

Several robustness results have unresolved reporting inconsistencies. Table 8's OAIMS(10) values match the PI-only results in Table 2, while the OAIMS(50) variant is unspecified. Table 10 describes worst-first ordering as extending the extreme Flair-to-ATLAS experiment, but its random-order results differ substantially from the preceding extreme-shift results and resemble the multi-modality-source experiment. These comparisons need explicit, consistent configurations.

The CCG radius ablation confounds spatial support with loss strength: Equation 3 normalizes by image size and click count rather than Gaussian weight mass, so increasing sigma also increases the effective contribution of CCG. Consequently, the experiments do not cleanly establish that neighborhood information, rather than stronger weighting, explains the improvement over single-pixel supervision. A matched-weight comparison is needed.

The contribution is primarily an empirical combination of pseudo-label learning, click-conditioned prediction consistency, and spatially weighted cross-entropy. Its broader applicability remains unverified because adaptation is tested only with a U-Net. The weak frozen Med-SA comparison does not establish effectiveness on modern promptable backbones. Together with the reproducibility and evaluation gaps, this leaves the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold despite promising results.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: using interactive corrections to improve medical segmentation under distribution shift, including adaptation across images rather than only within an image.

Reports substantial improvements over relevant adaptation baselines using the same pretrained backbone. For example, ten-click Dice improves over TSCA from 74.0 to 88.0 on BraTS T1 and from 64.0 to 86.0 on ATLAS.

The evaluation is relatively broad, covering fundus datasets, MRI modalities, and different pathologies. Ablations examine the adaptation stages and loss components, while additional experiments investigate erroneous clicks, poor initial predictions, mixed distributions, and return to the source domain.

The method is computationally lightweight. The clicks-to-target experiment provides useful evidence of interaction efficiency: on BraTS T1, average clicks to reach 80% Dice decrease from 10.60 with TSCA to 4.43.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is substantially incomplete. The manuscript omits essential settings such as optimizer, training and adaptation learning rates, training duration, detailed U-Net configuration, image resolution, and preprocessing. Most target dataset sizes and baseline tuning procedures are also unspecified. A promise to release code after publication does not resolve these omissions.

Clinical applicability is supported only indirectly. MRI evaluation selects the single slice with the largest ground-truth lesion area per case, excluding much of the difficulty of volumetric segmentation, small lesions, and lesion-free slices. All interactions are simulated; there is no evidence that actual users produce comparable improvements or consider the resulting pseudo-labels satisfactory.

Statistical reporting is insufficient for a stochastic, sequential adaptation method. Main results lack uncertainty estimates and a clear repeated-run protocol. Although Table 6 averages three seeds and an ordering stress test is included, variability across training seeds, click simulations, and stream orders remains largely unquantified.

The CCG ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed spatial mechanism. Equation 3 normalizes by image size and click count rather than Gaussian weight mass, so changing sigma also changes the effective loss strength. The single-pixel comparison therefore confounds spatial support with optimization scale; a matched-weight comparison is needed.

Some reporting inconsistencies weaken the robustness evidence. Table 8's OAIMS(10) values match the PI-only results in Table 2 rather than PI+MI, without identifying the variant used for the 50-click comparison. Table 10's random-order ten-click result is 86.0, whereas the preceding extreme-shift experiment reports 80.0; the text describes a continuation of that scenario without explaining the configuration difference.

The methodological novelty is incremental: pseudo-label adaptation, interaction-level updates, and Gaussian spatial weighting are combined effectively, but broader significance rests primarily on empirical validation. Only one backbone is adapted, and the markedly weaker frozen Med-SA comparison does not establish transferability to stronger contemporary interactive models. The promising results are not yet sufficient to outweigh the reproducibility and evaluation limitations.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: using interactive corrections to adapt medical segmentation models under distribution shift. The combination of post-interaction pseudo-label learning, mid-interaction updates, and click-centered weighting is intuitive and computationally lightweight.
Reports substantial improvements across multiple datasets, modalities, and pathologies. At 10 clicks, OAIMS improves over TSCA from 74.0 to 88.0 Dice on BraTS T1 and from 64.0 to 86.0 on ATLAS.
The main adaptation comparisons use the same pretrained backbone, including CCG pretraining, which helps isolate the contribution of online adaptation.

Extensive ablations examine adaptation stages, loss components, Gaussian weighting, and click budgets. Additional experiments address erroneous clicks, mixed domains, poor initial predictions, and return to the source domain.
The click-efficiency experiment provides useful evidence beyond fixed-budget Dice: reaching 80% Dice on BraTS T1 takes 4.43 clicks versus 10.60 for TSCA.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is insufficient. The manuscript omits important training and adaptation settings, including optimizer, learning rates, training schedule, precise U-Net configuration, and image preprocessing/resolution. Target sample counts and baseline tuning procedures are also inadequately documented. Code is only promised after publication.

Clinical applicability is overstated relative to the evaluation. All interactions are simulated using ground-truth error regions, and MRI evaluation selects only the largest-lesion slice per patient. This excludes much of the difficulty of volumetric segmentation, small lesions, and realistic clinician interaction. Synthetic incorrect clicks are useful but do not replace a user study.

Statistical support is limited. Most results lack variability estimates across seeds, click realizations, and image orderings; Table 6 reports three-run averages without dispersion. Aggregate sequence scores also obscure adaptation speed and whether performance deteriorates temporarily for individual patients.

Some robustness results contain unresolved inconsistencies. Table 8's OAIMS(10) values match the PI-only results in Table 2 rather than PI+MI, making the 10-versus-50-click comparison ambiguous. Table 10 describes the worst-first experiment as continuing the extreme-shift setting, but its random-order results closely resemble the different, multi-modality-source setting in Table 3.

The methodological advance is incremental over existing interactive adaptation and pseudo-label learning. The Gaussian-radius ablation does not cleanly isolate spatial context: because CCG is normalized by image area rather than kernel mass, changing sigma also changes the effective loss strength. A matched-strength single-pixel baseline would better support the central explanation.

Only one backbone is used to demonstrate the proposed adaptation method. The weak frozen Med-SA comparison does not establish architecture independence. Overall, the substantial empirical gains are promising, but the reproducibility and evaluation limitations leave the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.
